parties.summary: The statement was issued collectively at the 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 6 July 2025. The 2025 presidency lists 11 member States: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia, Indonesia and Iran. The official text has no individual signature block, so the record lists the member States and does not attribute a separate signature or a separate act of co-issuance to any of them. The presidency's membership page was read on 23 November 2026; it is a later snapshot of the presidency's list, used only for the composition at the summit and not as evidence that every listed State issued the statement. Saudi participation is recorded inconsistently by official sources: the presidency lists the Kingdom as a member, while the Saudi Press Agency reported on 7 July 2025 that the Foreign Minister led the delegation 'as an invited country to join the BRICS group'. The record states the conflict and does not resolve it by counting ten.

related.note: Both documents assert sovereignty and a UN-centred framework; the BRICS statement is a collective leaders' text, whereas China's initiative is a unilateral government proposal.
The BRICS statement precedes WAICO by a year and expresses a similar Global South capacity-building position, but it creates no institution and has no formal link to WAICO.
Both are non-binding summit statements with a development and access agenda; New Delhi is a wider summit declaration, while the BRICS statement is a coalition statement.
The UN's Global Digital Compact is the universal digital-cooperation framework; the BRICS statement is a separate coalition text that calls for the UN to be at the core of AI governance.

ai_provisions: Digital sovereignty and the right to development — all countries may adopt their own AI regulatory frameworks, develop AI capacities and pursue technological autonomy within their jurisdictions.
Global governance under the UN Charter — AI governance must respect national sovereignty, be representative, development-oriented, accessible and inclusive, and place the United Nations at its core.
Market regulation and data governance — personal data protection, information integrity and the rights and interests of humanity.
AI for sustainable development — innovation, productivity, sustainable practices and the reduction of digital and data divides within and between countries.
Capacity building — support for developing countries, technology transfer and access to AI technologies and skills.
Risk mitigation — collective action on safety, transparency, accountability and the risks arising from AI, without creating binding obligations.
International cooperation — the statement warns that a proliferation of initiatives and diverging views may aggravate asymmetries and the legitimacy gap in global digital governance.
relevance.excluded_scope: A political statement by BRICS leaders. It creates no binding obligation, no signature or ratification, no depositary, no monitoring or reporting duty and no dispute-settlement mechanism. It does not establish an institution or a follow-up mechanism. National implementation is not assessed.
relevance.reason: The first stand-alone BRICS leaders' statement on the global governance of artificial intelligence, issued at the 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 6 July 2025; the presidency lists 11 member States, the official text has no individual signature block, and Saudi participation is contested. It sets out a collective position centred on digital sovereignty, the right to development, the UN Charter, capacity building and the concerns of the Global South. It is a political statement, not a treaty: it creates no legal obligation, ratification, depositary or monitoring. It is included because it is a distinct coalition instrument that the three-pole reading would otherwise miss, and because it documents the China-Global South diffusion position before WAICO was established.

status_note: Non-binding political statement, not a treaty. It was issued collectively by the leaders of the BRICS member States at the Rio de Janeiro summit; the official text has no individual signature block. The record therefore counts 11 listed member States, not 11 signatories and not 11 individually evidenced co-issuers. The 2025 presidency lists Saudi Arabia as a member; the Saudi Press Agency described the Kingdom on 7 July 2025 as an invited country and said the Foreign Minister led its delegation. No document-specific list of issuing governments was located. No ratification, depositary, monitoring or enforcement is established.
